myth: You need a lot of money to start investing.
fact: Most mutual funds in India allow SIPs starting from as low as ₹100-500 per month. Starting small and consistently beats waiting until you have a 'big enough' amount.

myth: A company making record profit means its stock price will go up.
fact: Stock prices move on expectations, not just results. If the market already expected even better profit, a 'good' result can still send the stock down because it missed inflated expectations.

myth: Mutual funds are only for people who understand the stock market.
fact: That's exactly the point of a mutual fund — a professional fund manager makes the stock-picking decisions for you, within the fund's stated strategy and regulatory limits.

myth: Fixed deposits are risk-free and the best way to grow wealth.
fact: FDs carry very low default risk, but after accounting for tax and inflation, their real (inflation-adjusted) return is often close to zero or even negative over long periods.

myth: SIP guarantees profit no matter what.
fact: SIP reduces the risk of bad timing by averaging your purchase price over time, but it does not guarantee a profit — if the market is lower when you need the money than your average cost, you can still see a loss.

myth: You should stop your SIP when the market falls.
fact: A falling market means your fixed SIP amount buys more units at a lower price. Stopping a SIP during a dip is often exactly the wrong moment to pause, from a pure cost-averaging perspective.

myth: Gold always gives better returns than equity in the long run.
fact: Over most 15-20 year periods in India, well-diversified equity has historically outperformed gold, though gold has value as a portfolio diversifier and performs differently during certain crisis periods.

myth: Term insurance is a waste of money if you don't die during the policy term.
fact: Term insurance is designed purely to protect your family financially in the event of your death — like other insurance, 'not needing it' is the good outcome, not a wasted purchase.

myth: A higher NAV means a mutual fund is more expensive or 'overvalued.'
fact: NAV is just the per-unit price based on the fund's history and size — it says nothing about whether the fund's future returns will be good or bad, unlike a stock's price relative to earnings.

myth: You should always pick the mutual fund with the highest past returns.
fact: Past performance is not a reliable predictor of future returns, and today's top performer in a narrow category can easily become tomorrow's laggard once market conditions shift.

myth: Real estate always goes up in value.
fact: Real estate can and does stagnate or decline in specific markets for years, and it carries high transaction costs, poor liquidity, and ongoing maintenance costs that are easy to underestimate.

myth: You don't need health insurance if your employer provides group cover.
fact: Employer group cover usually ends the day you leave the job, often at the exact moment — a job loss or transition — when you're most exposed. A personal health policy continues regardless of employment.

myth: Credit cards are dangerous and should be avoided entirely.
fact: Used responsibly (paid in full every month), a credit card builds your credit history, offers fraud protection, and can offer rewards — the danger is specifically in carrying a revolving balance, not in having the card.

myth: You need to check your portfolio daily to invest successfully.
fact: Frequent checking is correlated with more panic-driven decisions, not better returns. Long-term investors often benefit more from reviewing quarterly or annually than daily.

myth: Only salaried people with a fixed income can invest systematically.
fact: Freelancers and business owners can and should build systematic habits too — automating a transfer to investments right after each payment received works even with variable income.

myth: Index funds are only for people who don't understand investing.
fact: Index funds are a deliberate, well-researched strategy used by sophisticated investors specifically because most actively managed funds fail to beat their benchmark index over long periods, after fees.

myth: Diversification means owning as many different mutual funds as possible.
fact: Owning 10-15 funds with overlapping holdings isn't real diversification — it often just adds complexity and tracking effort without meaningfully reducing risk versus 3-4 well-chosen funds.

myth: ULIPs are a good way to get insurance and investment in one efficient product.
fact: Because ULIPs split your premium between insurance cost and investment, you typically get less life cover than a term plan and lower investment growth than a pure mutual fund for the same premium.

myth: You should wait for the market to 'correct' before starting to invest.
fact: Trying to time a correction means you need to be right about both when it happens and when it ends — most investors who wait end up staying on the sidelines far longer than they planned.

myth: A financial advisor recommending a product means it's the best option for you.
fact: Many distributors earn a commission that varies by product, which can bias recommendations. Asking about fees/commissions upfront, or using a fee-only advisor, helps align incentives with your interests.

myth: Paying only the 'minimum due' on a credit card is a safe way to manage cash flow.
fact: Interest on the remaining balance is charged at some of the highest rates in consumer lending — often 30-45% annually — making 'minimum due only' one of the most expensive habits in personal finance.

myth: You should invest your emergency fund in equity for better returns.
fact: An emergency fund's job is to be available exactly when you need it, including during a market downturn. Equity can be down 20-30% at the worst possible moment, defeating the fund's entire purpose.

myth: If a stock's price has fallen a lot, it's now 'cheap' and a good buy.
fact: A falling price alone doesn't make something cheap — it needs to be assessed against the business's actual value and prospects. Some falling stocks are falling for good reason and keep falling further.

myth: NPS and PPF are basically the same thing.
fact: PPF is a fixed-interest, government-guaranteed debt instrument, while NPS is market-linked with an equity component and different withdrawal rules at retirement — they serve different roles in a portfolio.

myth: You should always choose the mutual fund with the lowest NAV because it's 'cheaper.'
fact: A lower NAV doesn't mean more value for your money — two funds with the same strategy and ₹10,000 invested will grow by the same percentage regardless of whether their NAV is ₹20 or ₹200.

myth: Day trading is how most people build serious wealth in the stock market.
fact: Multiple studies on retail trading accounts show the large majority of frequent day traders underperform a simple buy-and-hold approach after accounting for costs, taxes, and time spent.

myth: You can't lose money in a 'safe' debt mutual fund.
fact: Debt funds can still lose value from interest rate changes, credit downgrades, or defaults in the underlying bonds — 'debt' means lower risk than equity, not zero risk.

myth: Once you buy term insurance, you're covered for life.
fact: Term insurance covers you only for the specific policy term you chose (e.g., until age 60 or 70) — cover ends when the term ends unless you've bought a plan that specifically extends further.

myth: A bigger tax refund means you're good with your taxes.
fact: A large refund usually means you overpaid tax through the year and gave the government an interest-free loan — better tax planning often means a smaller refund, not a bigger one.

myth: You should max out your 80C limit only with PPF because it's '100% safe.'
fact: ELSS funds also qualify for 80C with a much shorter 3-year lock-in and historically higher return potential — safety and growth potential both matter when choosing among 80C options.

myth: Your salary slip's CTC is what actually lands in your bank account.
fact: CTC includes employer PF contribution, insurance, and other benefits that never hit your bank account directly — your actual in-hand salary is usually meaningfully lower than the CTC figure.

myth: Investing is gambling, so you might as well just save in a bank account.
fact: Gambling has a negative expected return by design; broad, diversified, long-term investing has historically had a positive expected return — the two are structurally different, not just a matter of luck.

myth: A stock split makes a company more valuable.
fact: A stock split just divides existing shares into more, smaller-priced shares — the company's total value and your proportional ownership stay exactly the same.

myth: If a mutual fund's past 1-year return is 40%, it will likely repeat that next year.
fact: Extraordinary short-term returns are often driven by a temporary rally in a specific sector or theme, which can just as easily reverse — chasing the hottest recent return is a common investing mistake.

myth: You should avoid equity completely after retirement.
fact: Retirees still typically need some equity exposure to keep up with inflation over a 20-30 year retirement — the usual advice is to reduce equity allocation with age, not eliminate it entirely.

myth: Health insurance claims are always rejected or difficult, so it's not worth buying.
fact: Most claim rejections trace back to specific, avoidable issues — undisclosed pre-existing conditions, missed documentation, or policy exclusions — rather than insurers rejecting valid claims arbitrarily.

myth: A higher salary automatically means better personal finances.
fact: Savings rate and spending discipline matter more than income level — many high earners have low or negative net worth due to lifestyle inflation, while modest earners with discipline build real wealth.

myth: You should redeem your mutual funds as soon as you see a profit.
fact: Selling purely because you're 'in profit' ignores your actual goal and time horizon — if the goal is still years away, staying invested usually serves the goal better than locking in an early gain.

myth: IPOs are always a great investment because the company is 'finally' public.
fact: IPO pricing is set by the company and its bankers to maximize what the company raises, not to maximize what you earn — many IPOs underperform the broader market in the years following listing.
